prompt:
Which statements about the median-of-medians algorithm are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: With groups of 5, the pivot has roughly three tenths of the input size elements on each side
options.explanation: Correct. Half the group medians are ≤ the pivot, and each brings two more smaller elements from its group: about three tenths of the input size.

options.text: The two recursive size fractions are one fifth and at most seven tenths, with linear partition work
options.explanation: Correct. One recursive call finds the median of the one fifth of the input size medians; the other continues on at most about seven tenths of the input size elements.

options.text: With groups of 3 instead, the same analysis gives only O(n log n)
options.explanation: Correct. For the simple groups-of-three analysis, the two recursive size fractions sum to one. This gives only a logarithmic-factor linear upper bound, rather than a linear guarantee.

options.text: It is usually faster than randomised quickselect in practice
options.explanation: No. The extra grouping and pivot selection often adds overhead; exact speed depends on implementation. Some hybrids use it as a fallback.

options.text: Introselect uses it (or a similar guaranteed method) as a fallback when quickselect makes poor progress
options.explanation: Correct. A linear fallback with a suitable progress budget can give worst-case linear work. Heap-fallback introselect need not; ordinary C++ nth_element requires only average linear complexity.

workedExample:
The key test for a recurrence of this shape is whether the fractions add up to less than 1:

```formula
T(n) ≤ T(an) + T(bn) + O(n)
a + b < 1  ⇒  T(n) = O(n)
where
T(n): the worst-case running time on n elements
n: the number of elements
a: the fraction of the input the first recursive call gets (1/5 for groups of 5)
b: the fraction the second recursive call gets (7/10 for groups of 5)
O(n): linear work done outside the recursive calls
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
⇒: "which guarantees"
<: less than
≤: less than or equal to
In words: if the recursive calls together get less than the whole input, each level does a shrinking fraction of the work and the total is linear.
```

| Group size | Combined recursive fraction | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Full input across both calls | O(n log n) |
| 5 | Nine tenths in both calls | O(n) |
| 7 | Six sevenths in both calls | O(n) |

When the two size fractions sum to less than one, the work per recursion level shrinks geometrically and sums to O(n). The guarantee costs extra work per element, which is why randomised quickselect is the default and median of medians the safety net.

prompt: Median of medians (groups of 5) runs on 1,000 distinct elements. Using the bound that at least three tenths of the input size minus six elements lie on each side of the pivot, what is the largest possible size of the recursive call after partitioning?

options.explanation: That would need a perfect median pivot. Median of medians guarantees only an approximate middle.
Correct. At least 294 elements are excluded by the bound on the opposite side, leaving at most 706; the worked card shows the calculation.
That uses only one fifth of the input as the excluded fraction; groups of five give a stronger three-tenths guarantee before rounding.
That's the worst case of plain quickselect (shrinking by a handful). Median of medians guarantees much more.

workedExample:
1. Groups: 1000 / 5 = 200 groups, so 200 medians.
2. The pivot M is the median of those 200, so about 100 group medians are ≤ M.
3. Each such group contributes its median and the 2 elements below it: 3 elements ≤ M. Excluding M's own group and edge effects gives the textbook bound:

```formula
s_min = 3n / 10 − 6
s_min = 3 × 1000 / 10 − 6 = 294
r ≤ n − s_min
r ≤ 1000 − 294 = 706
where
s_min: the conservative lower bound on elements excluded on either side of the pivot; here 294, not a measured actual count
M: the median of the group medians
n: the number of elements; here 1,000
r: the most elements the recursive call can receive (7 × n / 10 + 6)
≥: greater than or equal to
≤: less than or equal to
In words: at least 294 elements are on each side of M, so the side you recurse into has at most 706.
```

4. Same argument for ≥ M, so the recursive side has at most 706 elements.

Each round discards at least ~29% of the elements, guaranteed.
